items.title: TanStack Query: Server State That Stays Fresh Without the Boilerplate
items.summary: Two visitors open the same bookshop page a minute apart. The first one buys the last copy of a title. The second visitor's page still says one copy is in stock, because the data was fetched once at load and never checked again. She clicks buy, and the order fails at checkout. That gap is the problem TanStack Query is built for. Data from a server is not like the state inside your app. It lives somewhere else, it changes without telling you, it can fail to arrive, and a copy fetched five minutes ago may be wrong. TanStack Query keeps a cache of that server data, refetches it when it goes stale, and retries when a request fails. My judgement is that TanStack Query earns its place the moment two parts of an app need the same server data, or one screen needs that data to stay fresh. A single fetch on a page that never changes does not need it; a plain fetch inside useEffect does that job with less to learn. The value shows up when the same book list appears on the shop page and the checkout, or when an order should refresh the stock count. I would check five things before adopting it. items.title: User Reminders in Node.js: How Cron Triggers Webhook Tasks Explained
items.summary: The least complex design is a cron trigger that calls a public webhook, waits for that webhook to enqueue the reminder work, and lets an idempotent worker perform delivery. Cron decides when an attempt starts; it does not prove that every subscriber received a shipment update. The page fires at 09:00, but the useful signal is not “cron ran.” It is closer to “the scheduled run produced no accepted queue message” or “the queue has stopped making progress.” An on-call engineer should see a schedule identifier, the attempt status, and a request ID. The payload should contain only the reminder facts needed by the worker, not a full student record. Work backwards from that page. A publicly reachable cron URL invokes the webhook. The webhook validates the request, publishes one message per required subscriber, and returns a small success or failure status. The worker consumes each message, records a deduplication key such as shipment-update:shipment-1842:subscriber-77, and performs the delivery. If a runtime error occurs, log the failed attempt with the schedule, subscriber, and retry decision. That is the short answer. A cron expression is a clock, not a delivery guarantee. Start small.

items.title: Graceful Drain Over Hard Stops in Node.js Delayed Webhook Queue Recovery
items.summary: Short answer: For message queue timeout issues when delivering delayed webhooks, choose a graceful drain with durable checkpoints, not a hard stop followed by a blind retry storm. The drain keeps in-flight webhook attempts owned by a worker, releases work that has not started, and records the next retry time before capacity disappears. A hard stop is acceptable only when the queue can prove that every unstarted item remains invisible to consumers and every delivery attempt is idempotent. That is the operational recovery decision. The timeout is a symptom; the dangerous state is uncertainty about who owns a delayed webhook. My evaluation harness starts with 1,000 synthetic orders, 100 due webhook jobs, worker concurrency of 8, and a downstream response budget of 2 seconds. I vary downstream latency and interrupt the pool during each phase. I measure duplicate deliveries, lost retry deadlines, time to regain a stable queue, and oldest due-job age before copying the choice. Notebook-to-prod reasoning that skips recovery data usually optimizes the wrong failure. A delayed webhook has at least three clocks: its scheduled time, the attempt timeout, and the retry deadline. Short answer: put a monotonically increasing sequence number beside the host's playback position, reject observations older than the last applied sequence, and correct small drift by changing playback rate rather than seeking on every message. items.title: iOS Silent Push Notifications That Actually Arrive: content-available, Priority 5 and the Throttling Rules
items.summary: Silent push notifications (Apple calls them background notifications) are the push you send when you don't want to show anything. You just want the app to wake up, fetch new data, refresh a cache or sync a record. They're also the push type developers most often swear "doesn't work." Usually it does work. It just follows rules that visible alerts don't. This guide covers the exact payload and headers, the app-side code, and the reasons a silent push gets delayed or dropped. A silent push is a payload with content-available set to 1 and no alert, sound or badge: { "aps": { "content-available": 1 }, "type": "sync", "since": "2026-11-09T04:00:00Z" } Anything outside aps is your own data and is handed to the app. Keep the total under 4 KB. If you add an alert to the same payload, it's no longer a silent push. It becomes a visible notification that also happens to wake the app, and it follows the visible-alert rules instead. When you call APNs over HTTP/2, a background notification needs these headers: Header Value apns-push-type background apns-priority 5 apns-topic your app's bundle ID Two rules matter here: apns-push-type must be background. items.title: The same shipping event, twice, in two languages: a dedup rule we measured and did not ship
items.summary: If you store carrier scan events, you will eventually meet a timeline where every row appears twice: once in English, once in another script, with the identical timestamp. Some postal operators publish each event in more than one language, and if you persist what the carrier published, you persist both. The obvious fix is a dedup rule. This is the story of why we measured one, found it destroys real data, and shipped nothing. Most event tables end up keyed on something like: UNIQUE KEY uk_event (tracking_number, event_date, description) That key is wrong twice over. It under-dedups. items.title: Notes on generating QR codes for print: error correction, logo holes and quiet zones
items.summary: I work on sellphotos.online, where this was originally published. Every event on sellphotos.online gets a QR code. Photographers print it on posters, notice boards and table cards, or put it on the last slide at a prize-giving. Guests scan it in poor light, at an angle, through glare on a laminated sheet. We generate the codes ourselves with the small uqr encoder, then draw them with our own code. These are the decisions that came out of that. QR codes carry Reed-Solomon error correction at four levels. Roughly, these are the share of codewords that can be recovered: level recoverable L ~7% M ~15% Q ~25% H ~30% Higher levels need more modules for the same data, so at a fixed print size each module gets smaller. We use three levels, one for each place a code ends up: M for codes read off a screen. These are the UPI and Pix payment codes on a buyer's order page. A screen is flat, lit and clean. Q for printed event codes. Paper gets scuffed, laminate catches glare, and cheap printers blur edges. H when a logo sits in the middle, because the logo hides modules on purpose. items.title: Large PDF Export Downloads: 3 Telemetry Signals Behind Presigned URL Timeouts
items.summary: Pick the delivery path by export size, not by file type. A 40 MB pack of countersigned PDFs and a 300 KB CSV both come out of the same object storage bucket, and both get the same presigned URL treatment — but only the big one can lose a download to a link whose clock ran out mid-transfer. Under about 5 MB, hand the browser a signed link and move on. Above that, a large export needs three things before anyone clicks: a completion check on the object, a URL lifetime sized for your slowest connection, and range requests so a stalled transfer resumes instead of restarting from byte zero. The system I have in mind is a B2B SaaS document vault. Countersigned agreements land in a private bucket, each one carries an explicit deletion deadline, and customers pull quarterly packs that run from a few megabytes to a few hundred. Nobody reports "the presigned URL expired." They report "the download is slow and then it dies." items.title: We built a ChatGPT-style chat with no AI framework
items.summary: We built the AI chat in Sybill by hand, with ChatGPT as our reference. In January 2025 we started building Ask Sybill, the AI chat inside Sybill. Sybill makes AI tools for sales teams, and we wanted the chat to feel like ChatGPT, with the answer appearing word by word. AI chat frameworks were still young, and we did not use one. Instead, we opened ChatGPT in the browser and watched in the Network tab how an answer arrives: a stream of small events (Server-Sent Events), one after another. Then we built our own version of that stream. Today Ask Sybill keeps the answer when the connection drops, and you can run many chats at the same time. Getting there took much longer than we planned, and for a long time it felt like there was always one more thing to fix. At the end of January I wrote the code that reads those events while they arrive. For this I used an async generator: a function that hands out values one at a time and waits in between for more data. Most of us almost never write one. This is the integration failure mode I'd address first when adopting Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft. The repository combines shot recipes, motion previews, beat synchronization, and editable Remotion output. When those systems depend on valid composition data, partial updates become destructive operations. A dropped connection shouldn't be an editor state corruption incident. The streaming layer owns an expendable draft. The editor owns an explicitly accepted, validated plan. Remotion consumes committed composition data, never individual model tokens. items.title: Day 16: JSON-RPC 2.0: Protocol Choice and the Request Pipeline
items.summary: The previous post, API Contract Layering and the Type Registry, was about how the framework knows which type to build once a call arrives. The question one step earlier is what that call itself looks like. A system with a thousand forms has thousands of methods to expose, and the vast majority of them are the same set of actions applied to different forms. What the protocol has to decide is how they are addressed, how parameters travel, and how failure is reported. The framework's answer is one POST endpoint, one method string, and one pipeline in a fixed order. Each of those three decisions has a cost, and two positions on that pipeline are deliberately placed. This post covers: Why JSON-RPC rather than REST, and what that choice buys and gives up What each of the two payload layers holds, and why every exposed method takes exactly one parameter What one Ping round trip actually sends, and the four things the framework does not do the way JSON-RPC 2.0 specifies How the method string is cut into a ProgId and an action, and how each half is resolved The fixed stops one request passes through, and the one line that decides what failure looks like This is a choice, not a verdict. items.title: A Mute Button Must Fail Closed: Recording App and Microphone Audio with ReplayKit
items.summary: A screen recording can look correct while sounding completely wrong. A tutorial needs narration above the application’s audio; a demonstration may need only system sound. Treating both inputs as one volume control makes those two jobs unnecessarily difficult. In Reel Screen Recorder, the broadcast extension receives ReplayKit buffers and keeps their source identity until the writer dispatches them. The useful engineering detail is not the slider itself. It is what happens when transforming a buffer fails. The current SampleHandler.handleAudio distinguishes .audioMic from .audioApp and asks the shared settings for recordingGain(forMicrophone:). It then passes the processed buffer, with its original source type, to BroadcastWriter. The writer routes video, app audio, and microphone audio to separate capture functions. Its asset writer uses the MP4 container. This division keeps capture policy out of the file-writing dispatch code and makes it possible to reason about each source independently. items.summary: CrowdStrike's "Falcon Guardian" protects Windows systems by enforcing policy, restricting unauthorized applications and blocking USB devices, notes Gartner. And now CrowdStrike says they're giving security teams "the ultimate human control over AI agents" with — an "AI Kill Switch... a defender can terminate it where it runs, block it from launching again, and cut off its enterprise network access." "When you deploy agents with a kill switch, you stay in control," said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike... "The AI Kill Switch puts power in the hands of the people to realize AI safety...." In the case of a rogue agent, the AI Kill Switch will give the security decision-maker the final control: terminate the agent at its root, where it runs. It starts on the endpoint, where the Falcon sensor already operates, and builds on what Falcon Guardian already sees: what an agent is told to do, what it communicates, and what it executes... items.summary: I've been exploring Three.js and WebGL lately, experimenting with different ways to make websites more interactive. One thing I really enjoy about 3D on the web is that you're not limited to displaying objects. You can actually let people interact with them, explore them, and understand how things work. So I decided to build something around that idea. Meet Camera Lab — an interactive 3D experience where you can explore a DSLR camera, take it apart, and see what's happening inside. 📷 Instead of simply displaying a 3D camera that rotates, I wanted people to be able to explore the engineering behind it. items.title: I audited AI-built Supabase apps. These are the security bugs I keep finding
items.summary: Tools like Lovable, Bolt and Cursor can take you from idea to working app in a weekend. The demo works, the UI looks great, and you are ready to launch. But "it works" and "it's safe to put real users on it" are not the same thing. I audit React + Supabase apps built with AI tools, and the same problems show up again and again. Here are the five that matter most, and how to check your own app in a few minutes. This is the most serious one. A server function receives something like notebook_id or order_id from the request, then reads or writes data with the service role key, which bypasses Row Level Security. The function checks that the user is logged in, but not that the ID belongs to them. Any signed-in user can send someone else's ID and get their data. Fix: before using an ID from the request, look it up with the caller's own session (so RLS applies), or check ownership explicitly. Payment webhooks and "job finished" callbacks often run without any secret check. Anyone who finds the URL can send fake payments or overwrite records. The lawsuit, which refers to the girl as Emma, said that her parents first learned she had access to Google's AI in mid-March after their daughter's school sent a message warning them that she was in "imminent danger" of self-harm. Emma's mother logged into the teen's school Google account and found her daughter composing a suicide note on Google Docs, the complaint said. Her parents, named as John and Jane Doe in the lawsuit, immediately took Emma for an emergency psychiatric evaluation, and she now goes to therapy every week. Emma, a seventh grader in Charlotte, North Carolina, had grown convinced that she had multiple mental health disorders following interactions with AI Mode, a chatbotlike feature on Google Search, the complaint said. items.title: Quand le jumeau numérique rencontre la réalité moléculaire : mon plongeon VR dans NexoPeek
items.summary: Quand le jumeau numérique rencontre la réalité moléculaire : mon plongeon VR dans NexoPeek J’ai toujours détesté les slides PowerPoint qui vendent « la simulation temps réel » sans montrer le code. Le soir où j’ai ouvert le casque, la pièce sentait le café froid et le plastique neuf. Le projet : valider un circuit de signalisation MAP‑kinase avant la prochaine revue de design. L’architecture de NexoPeek sépare le moteur de physique (C++ / CUDA) du front‑end WebXR (Three.js + React). Le pipeline de données passe par un bus gRPC qui stream les coordonnées atomiques à 90 fps. items.title: Who wants to crowdsource LLM scans of articles submitted to Lobste.rs?
items.summary: Like many of us who value the human side of the web, I am looking for ways to keep slop at bay. It seems like LLM detection technology works reasonably well nowadays, with Pangram as the main provider. It is expensive, though! Assuming pangram scans are trustworthy, and it seems they are, we could create a centralized index of pangram scans of articles. I have already set up a prototype where I publish results of my own pangram scans. I could create more users, each tied to its own API key, so others can contribute with scans as well. This is way more resource efficient than everyone running their own scans. What do you think? Update: since this is receiving quite some attention, let me clarify one thing. I'm not proposing to change Lobste.rs itself. I'm wondering if there are enough people who'd like to join forces to maintain an independent index of pangram scans, for our own use, not intending to impose it on anyone (e.g., maybe we could have a browser extension that automatically shows the scan results for articles when browsing Lobste.rs or the orange site).

items.title: Branding a Multi-Tenant Admin From One Color: How the Palette Is Built
items.summary: Every store on StoreFlux gets its own admin dashboard, and store owners want it to look like their brand, not ours. That means the admin has to be themeable from a few inputs, and it has to stay readable when someone picks a color that is too light, too dark, or the wrong shade of blue. This is how the Admin Branding page works, and how the palette is built. The store owner picks a primary color. The admin generates an 11-step scale from it, labelled 50 to 950, the same shape Tailwind uses. The generator converts the hex color to HSL, keeps the hue and saturation, and sets lightness at fixed targets: 96% for step 50, falling to 20% for step 950. Lightness alone can make the ends of a scale look neon or muddy. So the generator lowers saturation at the very light and very dark steps, by 15 points near the top and 10 near the bottom, with a floor so those colors never turn grey. The palette is written as CSS custom properties on the root element. The primary color drives the indigo, blue, and sky utilities, and the accent drives violet and purple. items.title: Python's CVEs Triple. Anthropic Funds a New Security Developer
items.summary: In the last year CVEs have increased 3x for Python and its package manager Pip, according to Python's security developer in residence Seth Larson. "And the amount of malware published and removed from the Python Package Index (PyPI) is up 60%." Securing Python's ecosystem is getting more complex, he writes, especially given "the evolving role of AI in both security risks and security response." Their response includes bringing on a new Security Developer "to address the increasingly demanding scale of security response for the Python ecosystem." Providing prompt security response services and innovating to prevent future threats... is more difficult now than ever before... [Security developer Brett Smith] will help us keep pace with critical ongoing work such as vulnerability remediation, providing vulnerability data as a CVE Numbering Authority, and removing malware from PyPI. He'll also give the team bandwidth for new projects such as scaling PyPI's autonomous quarantine program to reduce manual effort on malware remediation and streamlining processes for the PSRT to handle the new vulnerability report volume. items.title: How I built Vicedex, a GTA 6 cheats and checklist companion
items.summary: GTA 6 comes out on 19 November 2026. Search for "GTA 6 cheats" today and most of what you find is GTA V codes with a new heading, or guesses. I wanted the opposite: a reference that lists a code only after someone has entered it on a retail copy of the game and watched it work. That rule became the product, and the tagline: Verified. Not guessed. Vicedex is two things: the website vicedex.app and a free iPhone app, GTA 6 Cheats, Map & Checklist. Here is how it is put together. Every cheat entry carries the date it was checked and a named source. The app shows a "verified" seal only on codes tested on GTA 6 itself. GTA V codes are in the app today, but they are labelled GTA V everywhere, carry "Checked" with a date instead of the seal, and live behind a separate switch so nobody mistakes one game for the other. The GTA 6 list ships empty. That sounds odd for a cheats app, but an empty list with a clear reason is more honest than a full one made of guesses. Cheats, the checklist, news, videos and guides are JSON files in the app repo. Connection strings with a SQL username and password end up in config files, pipelines and sometimes source control. With a managed identity, your Azure-hosted .NET app signs in to Azure SQL using Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) and gets tokens automatically. There is no secret to store, rotate or leak. Azure gives your App Service, Function App, container or VM an identity in Microsoft Entra ID. Your code asks for a token for that identity, and SQL Server accepts the token instead of a password. The client library handles token caching and renewal for you. In the Azure portal, open your App Service (or Function App), go to Identity, and switch System assigned to On. Azure creates an identity with the same name as the app. Or with the Azure CLI: az webapp identity assign --name payroll-api --resource-group rg-payroll Only a Microsoft Entra account can create Entra-based database users. items.summary: Most abandoned carts are not a decision to leave. Someone got distracted, the page felt slow, or they meant to come back and forgot. A single reminder catches some of them. A sequence catches more, as long as it stops the moment the shopper buys. Here is how the cart recovery sequence in StoreFlux works, using the default timings. There are three emails. The defaults are 1 hour, 24 hours, and 72 hours (60, 1440, and 4320 minutes). The first is a gentle reminder, the second is a second nudge the next day, and the third is the one that can carry a recovery discount. Each stage's timing is configurable per store. Before each send, the sweeper checks whether the cart has converted to an order. If the shopper completed checkout, the remaining emails are not sent. Nobody gets a reminder about a purchase they already made. The third email can issue a recovery coupon, but only when two things are both true: the store has the include-coupon setting turned on, and the Coupons module is enabled for that tenant. items.title: Stop Copying a String Into a MemoryStream. .NET 11 Has StringStream
items.summary: TL;DR: .NET 11 adds StringStream, ReadOnlyMemoryStream, and WritableMemoryStream. They wrap a string, a ReadOnlyMemory , or a Memory as a Stream, so you stop copying data into a MemoryStream just to satisfy a method signature. This ships in .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 2 with a go-live license, but is not GA yet. Everything below was run on the .NET 11 RC 1 SDK. Some API wants a Stream. You have a string. So you write the line that has been in every codebase since 2002: using var stream = new MemoryStream(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text)); It works. It also encodes the entire string into a brand new byte[] before the parser reads a single byte. The same story repeats with buffers. You already have a ReadOnlyMemory from a pool, a socket, or a slice, and the only way to hand it to a Stream API was to call ToArray() and copy it, or write your own little wrapper class. Most teams have that wrapper somewhere, usually named MemoryStreamButBetter. Four new Stream types that sit directly on top of memory you already have: StringStream reads a string or ReadOnlyMemory as bytes in the encoding you pick. items.title: I Threw Away 786 MB of Scratch Buffers
items.summary: I had a message processor that unpacked each incoming record into a scratch buffer, read one value out, and moved on. The buffer was pure throwaway: fill it, peek at a byte, forget it. I wrote the obvious thing, new byte[4096] at the top of the loop, and shipped it. It worked. It was also quietly handing the garbage collector a short-lived 4 KB array every single iteration, and I didn't notice until I was staring at an allocation profile for something else and saw this loop sitting near the top. Here's the loop, more or less: for (int i = 0; i keeps a stash of reusable arrays. You Rent one when you need it and Return it when you're done, and the same physical arrays cycle through your loop instead of a fresh one each pass. for (int i = 0; i .Shared.Rent(bufferSize); try { Fill(scratch.AsSpan(0, bufferSize), i); sink += scratch[i % bufferSize]; } finally { ArrayPool .Shared.Return(scratch); } } Same loop, same result. The allocation line: ArrayPool : 0.0 MB allocated, 0 gen0 collections Zero. Once the pool warms up, the loop stops allocating entirely and the GC has nothing to collect. items.title: Breathe as One: a two-phone co-op game you win by breathing together
items.summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge Breathe as One is a little co-op game for two people and two iPhones. You win by breathing together. You sit across from each other with your phones propped up, front cameras facing you. Each phone only watches its own player. The SmartSpectra SDK picks up the rise and fall of your chest and turns it into a live wave, and the two phones swap those waves over a private nearby connection. So both screens show the same thing: your breath in blue and your partner's in coral. As you settle into the same rhythm, the two lines drift toward each other's color until they melt into one lilac line. Getting there is the whole game. items.title: I Summed 400,000 Rows on Every Refresh
items.summary: I had a little dashboard endpoint that summed a sales table by region. Nothing clever: filter the rows, add up the amounts, return a number. It felt instant in dev, so I stopped thinking about it. Then I left the page open on a second monitor. It auto-refreshes every few seconds, and when I tailed the logs I watched the same region total get recomputed over and over, each refresh redoing work whose answer hadn't moved since the last one. The underlying data changes maybe once an hour. I was aggregating 400,000 rows dozens of times a minute to produce a number I'd already produced. The usual reflex is to reach for IMemoryCache and wrap the computation. That works, but it caches inside the handler, so you still pay for model binding, the handler invocation, and serializing the result every single time. What I actually wanted was for the whole response to come back without my code running at all. That's what output caching does, and it's been sitting in ASP.NET Core since .NET 7. I'd just never turned it on. You register the services, add the middleware, and opt an endpoint in. items.title: Microsoft Removes PC-to-PC Migration from Windows 11, Points Users to OneDrive-Based Backup
items.summary: Windows 11 offered a PC-to-PC Migration feature that "moved files and settings directly between two PCs over Wi-Fi or Ethernet," reports Ghacks. But according to an updated Microsoft support page, the tool is no longer available. "Microsoft's support documentation now redirects users to Windows Backup, a tool that relies on OneDrive cloud storage instead of a direct connection between two computers..." Windows Backup works differently. It requires a personal Microsoft account and backs up supported folders (Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Videos and Music) to OneDrive. Free OneDrive accounts include only 5GB of storage, and Microsoft's own promotional screenshot for Windows Backup shows 4.5GB of that allowance already in use. Years of photos, documents and downloads can exceed the free tier quickly. Windows Backup does carry some extras. It can remember installed apps, Wi-Fi networks, passwords and some settings to speed up setup on a new device. Apps still have to be reinstalled, and supported files are restored from the cloud. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the article. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. The obvious way to give everyone the same puzzle is to generate it on a server. I didn't want a backend. The game is fully offline, has no accounts and collects no data. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills. These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self?
